push.verdict: Pushing straight across, both are shoved apart. They take their own recoil, so neither push costs the pusher his grip: each pushes with the effort he uses (88.8 kN each), about 5 times what holds the other (17.7 kN each). They fly apart at 7.61 m/s each and slide about 4.89 m.

effort: Effort: 10% of their strength (each as hard as lifting 9.06 t). The hardest both can go while nothing around them breaks.Courtesy ceiling: 10% (lifting 9.06 t). Past that, both are shoved apart and slide past the nearest people 5 m away (Rex 5.12 m, Ollie 5.12 m).
happens: With They take their own recoil on, a shoving match is decided at the feet of the one being pushed. Each one’s push back goes to his source, so pushing costs him no grip: each pushes with the effort he uses. The other’s push on him is real (a contest lets force move), and only his feet hold against it. (That assumes each leans into the push; upright, a body tips over at a few hundred newtons.)Equal bodies on equal ground are always shoved apart with the power on: even the least effort the lab lets them use, enough to stand and walk (as hard as lifting 2.57 t each), is more than either one’s grip on any ground here (μ × his weight, μ at most 0.84, on gravel). So with the power on there is no dead heat between them.Each is pushed by the other’s push, less his own hold, over the shove’s stroke (2.44 m, an estimate) while their hands stay on each other; then each slides to a stop on his feet against friction and air drag. A real body would tumble; the lab keeps him upright.They take their own recoil: each one’s push back goes to the endless ocean (28,000 kg·m/s each, over the push), so none of it reaches the ground. His feet hand the ground only what they hold against the other’s push (5,700 kg·m/s each), a friction drag while he slides.
callouts: Each is strong enough to lift the other, so a real bout goes to whoever gets lower first and pushes upward, taking the weight off the other’s feet. The sim can’t model that.
math: Push = the effort he uses, if he can stand (They take their own recoil: pushing costs him no grip); 0 lying flat. Hold = min(strength, footing), or the footing alone if he is too heavy to stand; footing = μ × min(m g, what the ground under his feet bears). Bolted: unlimited, whatever his strength (the bolts hold, not his muscles). Both pushes beat the other’s hold: each is pushed by (the other’s push − his hold) over the stroke d = 2.44 m (the shove’s, an estimate), with momentum p = F t and relativistic speeds; slide x = m/(2k) ln(1 + k v²/R), k = ½ρ C_d A. Walk-out: a = min((push − loser’s hold) ÷ m_loser, (his footing − loser’s push) ÷ m_winner), capped at his running speed, over half the ring (3.47 m).

lift.verdict: Rex lifts Ollie overhead with 30× the force needed.
tiles: Ollie’s weight29.4 kN3 tTheir gravity0.00011 Noverhead, centres 2.29 m apartTotal needed29.4 kNRex has 890 kN
effort: All-out: no cap needed. Nothing the lab checks in this test can do harm here (nearest people and buildings 5 m away), so they go all-out.Courtesy ceiling: none. Nothing in this test does harm, even all-out, with the nearest people and buildings 5 m away. A lift is a slow, steady load, not a blow: the lab models no ground shaking, air blast or broken ground for it.
happens: The lift models a partner who lets himself be lifted: Ollie’s weight is all Rex holds up, and that weight rests on Rex’s feet (weight, not recoil). In a contest Ollie’s push down on Rex would be real, its push back going to Ollie’s own source, so a partner who fought the lift would make it harder; the lab doesn’t model that.The ground under Rex carries both of them: 94.9 kPa under his feet.
math: Their gravity: the larger of G m₁ m₂ / d² with Ollie overhead (d = 0.65 × Rex’s height + 0.1 × Ollie’s = 2.29 m) and 0.385 G m₁ m₂ / d_touch², the peak while Ollie rises from beside him (d_touch = 1.75 m, two balls of their volume touching; the most of y / (x² + y²)^1.5 along a vertical path is 0.385 / x²).
